title: Moules Marinières
subtitle: Mussels steamed in white wine with shallots and parsley
excerpt: Live mussels steamed open in a pot with white wine, shallots, garlic, and butter. One of the fastest hot main courses in French cooking, 10 minutes from pan to table. Serve with crusty bread to soak up the broth.
sourceNotes: Moules marinières is a dish of the French Atlantic coast, Brittany, Normandy, and the Vendée. Elizabeth David, A Book of Mediterranean Food (1950) and French Provincial Cooking (1960), gives the standard recipe. The name means 'sailor's style', and the dish is associated with the mussel-farming traditions of the bay of Mont-Saint-Michel and the Charente coast.

glossaryTerms.definition: Removing the fibrous beard (byssus threads) that mussels use to attach to rocks. Grip the beard between thumb and forefinger and pull firmly toward the hinge end of the mussel. Do not debeard mussels too far in advance — the mussel dies soon after debearding and should be cooked within an hour.

content.text: Moules marinières is the fastest substantial hot dish in French cooking. Mussels go into a pot with wine, shallots, and garlic; the lid goes on; in 5 minutes every mussel is open and the pot is full of a concentrated, naturally briny broth. The only preparation is cleaning the mussels,
and scrubbing the shells, which takes about 10 minutes. Allow 500 g of mussels per person as a main course.

items.prepNote: scrubbed and debearded, closed ones only
divided: half for cooking, half to finish

content.text: Scrub the mussels under cold running water, scraping off any barnacles with a knife. Pull away the beards by gripping and pulling toward the hinge end. Discard any mussels with cracked or broken shells, and any that are open and do not close when firmly tapped. Mussels that remain open despite tapping are dead and must not be used.
Melt 20 g of the butter in the large pot over medium heat. Add the shallots and garlic and cook for 3 minutes until soft but not coloured.
Turn the heat to high and add the wine. Bring to a rolling boil. Tip in all the mussels at once and put the lid on. Steam for 4 to 5 minutes, shaking the pot twice, until all the mussels are open.
Discard any mussels that have not opened. Add the remaining 20 g of butter and the parsley. Shake the pot to combine. Taste the broth and season, it may not need salt.
Divide between two large warmed bowls and pour the broth over the mussels. Serve immediately with crusty bread.

items.symptom: Some mussels have not opened after 5 minutes
items.cause: A small number of mussels take longer or are dead.
items.fix: Remove the open mussels first. Return the closed ones to the pot with the lid for another 2 minutes. Any still closed after that are dead, discard them.

items.cause: The mussels were not rinsed thoroughly, or sand from inside the shells has released during cooking.
items.fix: Leave the last centimetre of broth in the pot when pouring into bowls, the sand sinks to the bottom. For very sandy mussels, strain the broth through a fine sieve before pouring over the mussels.

items.cause: They were overcooked, 2 to 3 minutes beyond the point all are open.
items.fix: Mussels are cooked the moment they open. Remove them from the pot as soon as the shells are open, even if it means doing this in batches. Returning to the heat for any longer than necessary toughens them.

content.text: The French Atlantic coast, from the bay of Mont-Saint-Michel southward through Brittany, the Vendée, and the Charente, is one of the world's largest mussel-farming regions. The rope-farmed mussels (moules de bouchot) of Mont-Saint-Michel carry a Protected Designation of Origin and are considered the finest in France. Moules marinières is the simplest and most universal way to cook them. The same basic recipe, in countless slight variations, appears on menus from the smallest coastal café to Parisian brasseries.
